headline: Thailand's Free Airport Layover Tours Suit Efficient Explorers, Not Wanderers
snippet: For millions of passengers whose layovers in Thailand currently amount to nothing more than time lost in an airport terminal, a pilot program launching in January 2027 will transform that waiting period into a short, cost-free excursion. The initiative, designed for transit passengers with six to eight hours between flights, allows travelers to exit the secure zone and explore the country without paying for a tour, provided they return in time for their connection. The move is driven by sheer volume. Tapani Kiatphaiboon, the head of the Thailand Tourism Authority, noted that Suvarnabhumi Airport alone handles approximately 1.3 million transit passengers annually. By targeting just 10% of this figure for the free tour program, Thailand aims to convert a logistical necessity into a revenue-generating cultural experience. The pilot will operate across four major hubs: Suvarnabhumi, Don Mueang, Phuket, and Krabi. The trade-off of the transit window The practicality of the program hinges on the specific constraints of the passenger's schedule. The tours are not generic city tours but are structured into three distinct categories designed to fit within the tight transit window: cultural-historical visits, culinary experiences, and wellness treatments. Options include the Grand Palace, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha, or the ancient site of Somut Pra Kaeo. Alternatively, passengers can engage with Thai street food culture or opt for spa procedures and traditional massage.

headline: Bulgaria Must Build Fiscal Buffers Against Shocks, Businesses Should Increase AI Adoption, IMF Managing Director Georgieva Says
snippet: Bulgaria should seek ways to reduce its budget deficit of 5% of GDP, as one-off fiscal measures do not provide a systemic solution, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said in an interview with BTA at the conclusion of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. In a world facing increasingly frequent external shocks, countries need to build buffers, while revenue policies should be aligned with the structural needs of their budgets, she noted. The Annual Meetings in Bangkok took place against the backdrop of the IMF's assessment that the global economy remains resilient, although accumulating risks are limiting its capacity to absorb further shocks. Asked about one-off fiscal measures, including the proposed excessive profits tax, Georgieva noted that such measures can help but do not constitute a systemic solution. According to her, building fiscal buffers requires revenue policies that generate sufficient resources to meet the budget's long-term needs. She also called for a more cautious fiscal policy amid inflation, as higher government spending generates additional demand and puts upward pressure on prices. Georgieva pointed out that inflation is being driven not only by high energy prices, which are likely to remain elevated for some time, but also by rising defence spending, ongoing trade tensions and stronger demand associated with artificial intelligence. She described inflation as a tax on low-income earners and noted that monetary policy needs to be more restrictive. She also said she expects the European Central Bank to introduce further interest rate hikes. In its October forecast, the IMF lowered its projection for Bulgaria's economic growth in 2026 to 2.6%, down from 2.8% in its April forecast. For 2027, the Fund raised its growth forecast from 2.5% to 2.7%. Georgieva also commented on the consequences of the changing security environment. According to her, the period following the end of the Cold War, when countries benefited from low defence spending, has come to an end. Russia's invasion of Ukraine and developments in the Middle East demonstrate that the world has become more insecure and that countries must adapt to the new circumstances. Georgieva noted that it would be more effective for Europe to increase defence spending collectively rather than for each country to act independently. The IMF recommends a larger European budget that would allow countries to jointly finance their shared priorities. According to her, these are long-term trends to which Europe must adapt. The IMF Managing Director also discussed Bulgaria's role in the development of artificial intelligence. She described the country's well-developed information technology sector as a strong foundation but noted that Bulgaria would not become a producer of the most advanced artificial intelligence models. The country can participate in supply chains, but the most important priority is to use the technology to increase labour productivity. According to Georgieva, Bulgaria needs to improve workforce skills and its education system, while expanding the use of artificial intelligence in small businesses and government institutions. She noted that Bulgaria and Europe lag behind the United States in labour productivity and that broader adoption of new technologies is essential to improving competitiveness. Here follows the full text of the interview: Q: Ms Georgieva, you recently warned that external shocks and the fragmentation of the global economy could keep energy and commodity prices elevated for some time. In light of these forecasts, what buffers should Bulgaria include in its 2027 budget to ensure that the economy remains resilient and that citizens’ real purchasing power is protected against renewed price pressures? In this context, how does the IMF view one-off fiscal measures, such as an excessive profits tax? A: It is clear to everyone around the world that inflation is higher and is expected to remain elevated. This is not only because of high energy prices, which are likely to stay high for some time, but also because many countries are increasing their defence spending, trade tensions have not subsided, and artificial intelligence is generating greater demand. All of this is driving prices up. Bulgaria is no exception. What does this require? First, it requires a more restrictive monetary policy. We cannot allow inflation to continue rising. Inflation is a tax on low-income people, who feel its effects most acutely. In Bulgaria’s case, we should expect that the European Central Bank may raise interest rates a little further in response to inflation in order to combat it. At the same time, fiscal policy must be very cautious because when it is more generous in an inflationary environment, it creates additional demand and pushes prices higher. In Bulgaria’s case, as we know, the deficit stands at 5%. We need to find ways to bring it down. One-off measures help, but they are not a systemic solution. If we want to build buffers in a world of more frequent external shocks, this means that revenue policy must be aligned with the structural needs of the budget. During these meetings, we discussed the need to build buffers. We now know that shocks occur frequently, and without such buffers, the consequences are more painful for both the economy and the people. We also discussed the need for this to be done everywhere, not just in Bulgaria. We need to rethink income policy and understand what we should do with taxation in the age of artificial intelligence. Whom do we tax, how do we tax them, and how much do we tax them? This is an issue that also needs to be considered in Bulgaria. Q: What kind of tax policy do we need in a world of more frequent shocks? What kind of tax policy do we need in a world where technology is rapidly changing the relationship between capital and labour? In my view, this will be an extremely important issue for the sustainability of public finances in the coming years. In recent weeks, there have been attacks on vessels located within our country's exclusive economic zone. From your perspective, how will these developments affect economic growth in Bulgaria and the region? A: What we know is that in a world of growing tensions, related not only to geopolitics but also to technology, it is important to think about security in ways we did not have to before. Following the end of the Cold War, we enjoyed three decades of a peace dividend stemming from low defence spending. That period is over. When Russia invaded Ukraine, it became clear that countries could no longer continue shaping their policies on the assumption that the world would remain peaceful. Events in the Middle East have once again confirmed that we live in a more complex world. It is multipolar, with many centres of influence, but it is also more insecure. Unfortunately, this means that more resources must be allocated to defence. For Europe, the best approach is to do this together. At the IMF, we recommend a larger European budget so that countries can work together on issues of common concern rather than each country spending independently, which is less efficient. Countries must work together. Let us see how the discussions on the EU budget conclude. For now, however, it seems that Europe has not yet fully recognised that these are long-term trends requiring it to adapt to the new world. Q: Where do you think Bulgaria stands on the global artificial intelligence map? A: Bulgaria has a very well-developed information technology sector. Let us remember that when we emerged from the planned economy, Bulgarians already had a notable presence among both hackers and IT specialists. This has since evolved into a dynamic information technology sector in our country. This puts us in a good position, but we should not deceive ourselves. We will not be producers of the most advanced artificial intelligence models, but we can be part of the supply chain precisely because we have this information technology sector in the country. The most important thing, however, is not to produce or supply artificial intelligence, but to use it. Bulgaria still has work to do when it comes to the adoption of artificial intelligence. We need to assess where we are well positioned and where improvements are needed. We have good digital infrastructure. In this respect, Bulgaria is well positioned. People have access to the internet, but we are not sufficiently prepared when it comes to developing people's skills and transforming the education system. This is a different world, and we need to change very quickly to adapt to it. We also have more work to do in helping small businesses use artificial intelligence as a means of increasing labour productivity. Bulgaria and Europe lag behind the United States in labour productivity. Over the past decades, Europe's income level has fallen to 70% of that in the United States. If we fail to expand the use of artificial intelligence so that it benefits every business and every government institution and increases labour productivity, we will not be able to make progress or remain competitive, either as the European Union or as Bulgaria. As I said earlier, we have a good foundation. We need to consider how to use it to transform the country's entire economy.

headline: Trump’s eleventh-hour midterm threat a setup for a bigger lie: legal expert
snippet: The Trump administration’s “unprecedented” escalation in its campaign to exert more control over the midterms is part of a grander scheme to create a contingency plan should Republicans suffer a “devastating” election loss, legal expert Joyce Vance theorized Saturday. “That’s what we need to be on guard for here,” Vance wrote in an analysis published Saturday night on her Substack. “Trump is already laying the groundwork to claim another election was stolen, rather than accept a result he doesn’t like.” This week, the Justice Department demanded that California not send ballots to a list of individuals it suspected were noncitizens, along with several other demands. The DOJ gave California officials 48 hours to comply under threat of legal action, which the agency followed up on Thursday. However, as flagged by Vance, who previously served as the U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, it seemed “pretty obvious” that the Trump administration’s plan was doomed to fail given the proximity to the midterms and legal precedents against making sweeping election changes. That the plan was doomed to fail, however, may be the point, Vance theorized. “It seems far more likely that what’s happening here is that the administration is setting up a narrative for after the election about how it was stolen,” Vance wrote. “What if the whole goal here is to have the courts slap down the case, so that Trump can argue, after a potentially devastating loss for Republicans at the polls, that it happened because the courts refused to stop noncitizens from voting even though he begged them to?” Vance continued: “It wouldn’t be true, but when has that ever stopped this president? That kind of pernicious narrative fits with the guy who perpetrated January 6 and who has never felt compelled to stick to the confines of the truth when talking about election outcomes.”

headline: FSSAI moves to ban sucrose and fructose in foods for infants up to six months
snippet: New Delhi, Oct 17 (IANS) The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has published a draft amendment that would prohibit the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age, an official statement said on Saturday. The statement from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare said the draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations, 2026, aims to strengthen nutritional safeguards for infants. The amendment published in the Gazette of India on October 16, 2026, would strengthen the existing regulatory framework by ensuring infant nutrition products are formulated to meet age‑appropriate requirements and minimise early exposure to added sugars. The draft notification has been published for public consultation, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders within 60 days. Custom Ad: Multiplex The representations received within the prescribed period will be considered by FSSAI before finalisation of the amendment. The existing regulations prescribe comprehensive nutritional composition, quality and safety standards for various categories of infant nutrition products intended for children from birth up to 24 months of age. Under the current provisions, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred sources of carbohydrates, while sucrose or fructose may be added only when required as a carbohydrate source, subject to prescribed limits. Building upon these provisions, the draft amendment proposes a specific restriction on the addition of sucrose and fructose in products intended for infants up to six months of age, the statement noted. The first six months of life represent a critical period for healthy growth and development, making appropriate nutrition particularly important. The proposed restriction seeks to ensure that infant nutrition products meet the nutritional needs of this age group and support broader public health efforts to address dietary risk factors linked to childhood obesity and related health challenges. The initiative complements established public health recommendations promoting exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life. The amendment will support appropriate infant feeding practices while encouraging manufacturers to adopt formulations that prioritise the specific nutritional requirements of young infants. —IANS aar/ag

headline: McConnell refusing to share millions in campaign cash with desperate colleagues: report
snippet: Despite the threat that Republicans could lose their majorities in both the House the Senate, former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) is refusing to lift a finger to help his colleagues, according to reporting. The Washington Sun reported that McConnell, the former Senate majority leader who took his seat in 1985, is “hoarding his committee’s wealth” during a crucial midterm cycle for Republicans, citing a new federal filing. When he returned to the Senate in September after a three-month, health-related absence, his campaign committee held nearly $7.4 million, the outlet said. McConnell, who announced in February 2025 that he would not seek an eighth term, has not given any of it to a Republican Party committee or candidate campaign, the Sun reported. That includes the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD), who succeeded McConnell as the party’s Senate leader. McConnell leaves the Senate in January, and the Sun laid out what his committee can still do with the surplus. It can give up to "$2,000 apiece to other Republican candidate committees." It can transfer unlimited amounts to national party committees such as the Republican National Committee or the National Republican Senatorial Committee. It can also donate to charities or nonprofit universities, refund donors, or send the money to the U.S. Treasury’s general fund, the outlet said. McConnell returned on Sept. 14 after being hospitalized in June. He has said he fell at home, was “briefly unconscious” and later contracted pneumonia.

headline: Callio Therapeutics Wins Best New ADC Drug Developer at the 13th World ADC Awards, Presents Across Five Sessions at World ADC San Diego
snippet: Callio leaders delivered three presentations and two panel discussions on dual-payload ADC resistance, manufacturability, linker design, and the path to next-generation ADCs SAN DIEGO, SEATTLE and SINGAPORE, Oct. 15, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Callio Therapeutics ("Callio" or "the Company"), a global, clinical-stage biotechnology company advancing dual-payload antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) as the next frontier of rationally designed targeted cancer therapy, today announced it has won Best New ADC Drug Developer at the 13th World ADC Awards. The award was presented at the World ADC Awards Gala on Wednesday evening, October 14, held during World ADC San Diego 2026. Callio also delivered three presentations and two panel discussions at the conference. Powered by a proprietary platform featuring modular, adaptable linker technology, Callio is actively developing a pipeline of dual-payload ADCs with rationally selected payload combinations designed to overcome treatment resistance in hard-to-treat tumors. CLIO-8221 is the first program from Callio's dual-payload ADC pipeline to enter the clinic, with the first patient dosed in March 2026, approximately one year after the Company's launch. "We are honored to accept this award, as this recognition reflects what the Callio team has built as we advance dual-payload ADCs for patients whose cancers stop responding to current therapies," said Zachary Hornby, Chief Executive Officer of Callio Therapeutics. "World ADC has emerged as the premier forum for the ADC community to come together and share the latest advancements in the field." Callio's Presence at World ADC San Diego 2026 The 17th World ADC San Diego summit brought together more than 1,300 industry attendees from over 400 companies, with seven tracks of end-to-end ADC content from discovery through manufacturing and supply. Callio's leadership and scientific team participated in the following panel discussions and presentations: Presentation: Harnessing the Promise of Dual-Payload ADCs to Combat Resistance to Traditional ADCs Presenter: Chris Hassig, PhD, Chief Scientific Officer Presentation: Leveraging a Modular & Adaptable Linker Design to Evaluate Translation of Rationally Selected Dual-Payload Combinations Presenter: Alyson Smith, Vice President of Research Panel Discussion: What's the New Path to the Next Generation of ADCs? Panelist: Jeremy Sauer, Vice President of Strategy Panel Discussion: Building the Next Generation of ADC Linkers & Payloads: What Do Innovators Need from Development & Manufacturing Partners? Panelist: Srinath Thirumalairajan, Executive Director of CMC Presentation: From Complexity to Manufacturability: Considerations to Rapidly Develop & Manufacture Dual-Payload ADCs Presenter: Srinath Thirumalairajan, Executive Director of CMC About Callio Therapeutics Callio Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biotechnology company that is developing dual-payload antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) as the next frontier of targeted cancer therapy to address high incidence tumors where better therapies are needed. Its proprietary platform pairs modular, adaptable linker technology with rationally selected synergistic payload combinations designed to block key resistance mechanisms that enable cancer's escape. The Company's lead clinical program, CLIO-8221, is a HER2-targeted dual-payload ADC with potential to prevent and overcome treatment resistance that limits efficacy of current ADCs. Located in San Diego, Seattle, and Singapore, backed by top life science investors, and led by an experienced team with a track record of ADC development and oncology drug approvals, Callio Therapeutics is built to deliver the next generation of dual-payload ADCs and better outcomes for people living with cancer. For more information, visit www.calliotx.com and follow Callio Therapeutics on LinkedIn. About CLIO-8221 HER2 is a clinically validated target for antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), with multiple approved therapies demonstrating clinical benefit across tumor types. However, most patients eventually progress on treatment despite their tumors retaining HER2 expression. Mechanistic resistance to cytotoxic payloads has emerged as a key driver of treatment failure. CLIO-8221 is a novel, first-in-class, dual-payload ADC targeting HER2, designed to overcome emergent resistance. CLIO-8221 delivers two mechanistically complementary payloads, a topoisomerase 1 (Topo1) inhibitor and an ATR inhibitor, directly to HER2-expressing tumors. While Topo1 inhibitors have shown strong clinical activity, activation of the DNA damage response following Topo1 inhibitor-induced replication stress represents a potential major driver of resistance. By simultaneously inhibiting Topo1 and blocking the DNA damage response through ATR inhibition, CLIO-8221 is engineered to overcome payload insensitivity and further sensitize tumors to Topo1 inhibition. Developed using proprietary linker and ADC platform technologies, CLIO-8221 aims to maximize anti-tumor activity while reducing systemic toxicity, offering the potential for deeper and more durable responses in patients with HER2-expressing tumors. CLIO-8221 is currently being evaluated in an ongoing Phase 1/2, first-in-human, dose-escalation and expansion study in adult patients with metastatic or unresectable HER2-expressing solid tumors, including those who previously received trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd). The first patient was dosed in March 2026, and enrollment is ongoing in Australia and the US, with plans to open the study in China (NCT07300943). Copyright 2026 GlobeNewswire, Inc.

headline: Punjab unveils BDS admission roadmap for 2026–27, with 1,100 private dental seats
snippet: LAHORE: Students hoping to pursue dentistry in Punjab now have a clearer picture of the road to admission after the provincial government formally notified its MBBS and BDS admission policy for the 2026–27 academic session, confirming dental seat allocations, eligibility requirements, merit rules and a separate admission timetable for public-sector BDS programmes. The notification, issued by the Punjab Specialized Healthcare and Medical Education Department on October 14, places the University of Health Sciences (UHS), Lahore, in charge of centralised admissions to public and private medical and dental colleges. For prospective dental students, the announcement brings several important decisions into focus: whether their academic record meets the minimum requirements, how they should rank their preferred institutions, and what financial commitments they must be prepared to meet if they receive an admission offer. The accompanying UHS public-sector admission notice schedules BDS applications from December 15 to 30, 2026, with dental classes expected to begin on March 1, 2027. Punjab lists 1,100 private BDS seats across 18 colleges One of the most significant figures in the admission notification concerns the number of places available at private dental institutions. According to the official allocation, 1,100 BDS seats have been listed across 18 private dental colleges in Punjab for the upcoming academic session. The institutions are located across several cities, including Lahore, Rawalpindi, Multan, Faisalabad, Sialkot, Sheikhupura, Sargodha and Lodhran. The approved intake figures listed for individual private dental colleges range from 50 to 75 seats, providing prospective applicants with a starting point for evaluating their options. Among the institutions named in the allocation are FMH College of Medicine and Dentistry, Lahore Medical and Dental College, Rashid Latif Dental College, Watim Dental College, Margalla Institute of Health Sciences and other private institutions offering dental education. The same provincial notification lists 4,400 MBBS seats across 33 private medical colleges, taking the combined private-sector MBBS and BDS allocation to 5,500 seats. For the public sector, UHS has identified four dental institutions in its admission notice: de'Montmorency College of Dentistry, Lahore; Nishtar Institute of Dentistry, Multan; Dental Institute, Punjab Medical College, Faisalabad; and the dental college at Quaid-e-Azam Medical College, Bahawalpur. The public-sector seat allocations remain subject to the relevant regulatory approvals. Applicants should consult the final UHS prospectus and approved college-wise intake before treating any listed seat figure as a guaranteed admission opportunity. What BDS applicants need to qualify The provincial policy establishes a minimum 50 per cent MDCAT passing score for BDS admission, compared with 55 per cent for MBBS. However, passing the entrance examination alone will not secure a place at a dental college. Candidates must also have obtained at least 60 per cent marks in FSc Pre-Medical, HSSC or an equivalent recognised 12th-grade qualification. Biology and Chemistry must form part of their qualifying subjects, together with either Physics or Mathematics. Applicants presenting equivalent qualifications must fulfil the applicable equivalence requirements, including certification by the Inter Boards Coordination Commission (IBCC), where required. The policy further specifies that MDCAT results remain valid for three years from the date of the examination, in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements. For students comparing medical and dental career paths, the difference between the qualifying MDCAT thresholds is particularly relevant. A candidate meeting the BDS threshold but falling below the MBBS requirement may still satisfy the dental programme's minimum MDCAT condition, provided all other eligibility requirements are met. How will BDS merit be calculated? Competition for dental college places will be determined through the same academic weighting formula used for MBBS admissions. The notified merit calculation is: MDCAT examination: 50 per cent FSc Pre-Medical/HSSC or equivalent: 40 per cent Matriculation/SSC or equivalent: 10 per cent This means half of a candidate's admission aggregate will come from MDCAT performance, making the entrance examination a major factor in determining merit position. The remainder will be drawn from higher-secondary and secondary academic results. The policy also confirms that additional marks will not be awarded for Hafiz-e-Quran status, consistent with the applicable regulatory framework and judicial ruling. Candidates should distinguish between minimum eligibility and competitive merit. Securing the required qualifying marks allows an applicant to be considered, but admission ultimately depends on aggregate merit, available seats, eligible admission categories and institutional preferences. BDS admissions to open in December; first merit list due in January Dental applicants have a different application calendar from MBBS candidates under the UHS public-sector admission notice. Online BDS applications are scheduled to open at 9am on December 15, 2026, and close at 5pm on December 30, 2026. The provisional merit order is scheduled for January 6, 2027, followed by the final merit order on January 9. The first college-wise BDS selection list is expected on January 11, 2027. Further selection and upgradation lists are scheduled for January 15 and January 21, allowing vacant seats to be filled according to merit and the preferences submitted by eligible candidates. Dental classes are scheduled to commence on March 1, 2027. For comparison, public-sector MBBS applications run from October 16 to October 30, 2026, with medical classes scheduled to begin on February 1, 2027. The published timetable is subject to subsequent directions from the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) and the Punjab government. Importantly, these dates relate to the public-sector admission notice. Candidates seeking private dental college admission should follow the separate private-sector schedule issued by UHS rather than assume that the same application window applies. Private dental college applicants face Rs600,000 initial deposit Alongside merit requirements, the financial conditions attached to admission are likely to be a major consideration for prospective BDS students and their families. Under the notified policy, candidates selected for private-sector medical or dental colleges must deposit Rs600,000 in the designated UHS bank account within three working days of the publication of the relevant merit list. The payment is required to secure the offered admission seat. Candidates who fail to deposit the prescribed amount within the specified period will lose their admission offer, and the vacant seat may be allocated to another eligible applicant according to merit. The initial deposit will subsequently be transferred to the concerned institution following completion of the admissions process. Any remaining fee must be paid directly to the college, with the policy allowing tuition payments on a quarterly, six-monthly or annual basis under the applicable regulations. For public-sector MBBS and BDS students, annual tuition has been fixed at Rs50,000, excluding students admitted against overseas or foreign quota arrangements and any separately applicable charges. UHS will also charge a non-refundable Rs2,000 application processing fee. Candidates applying for both MBBS and BDS are required to submit separate applications. For families considering private dental education, understanding the initial deposit requirement is especially important because an admission offer alone does not secure a seat without payment and completion of the prescribed joining formalities. College preference lists could decide where students study dentistry Beyond examination scores and seat availability, the policy places considerable importance on the order in which applicants choose their colleges. Candidates must enter their institutional preferences through the UHS online admission system. Those applying to public-sector institutions must arrange the available colleges according to their preferred order, while the policy does not restrict the number of private-sector institutions that an applicant may select. However, the rules contain an important condition: any institution left out of a candidate's preference list will not be considered for admission or subsequent upgradation. Although candidates may edit their applications before the submission deadline, the number and order of college preferences cannot be changed once the application period closes. This makes the selection process more than a formality. Students considering dentistry will need to weigh institutional preferences against practical factors such as location, affordability, living arrangements and their willingness to accept a particular college. The policy provides for successive merit and selection lists through which vacant seats may be offered to eligible candidates according to merit and submitted preferences. Private-sector students may also elect to give up their right to subsequent upgradation when joining an institution. Once exercised, this option cannot be reversed. Reserved seats and overseas admission arrangements The admission framework includes provisions for students applying against reserved and special admission categories. These cover eligible candidates with disabilities, applicants from notified under-developed districts, Cholistan residents and candidates seeking admission through specified arrangements involving other provinces and regions. The notification also addresses overseas Pakistani and dual-national applicants, as well as candidates admitted through designated foreign admission arrangements. Private-sector medical and dental colleges may reserve up to 15 per cent of their annual intake for eligible overseas Pakistani or dual-national expatriate candidates. If seats reserved under that category remain vacant because of a lack of eligible applicants or other reasons, they must be transferred to open merit, with the relevant fee structure applying. In public-sector institutions, candidates admitted against overseas Pakistani quota seats are required to pay US$10,000 annually under the self-financing arrangement. Overseas Pakistani applicants who secure ordinary open-merit seats, however, are required to pay fees applicable to Pakistani students. The detailed policy also establishes additional documentation and assessment requirements for specific reserved categories. Students applying under any such arrangement should examine the relevant eligibility provisions rather than rely solely on the general admission criteria. Admission process to remain online UHS will administer the centralised process through its online admissions system, using separate application arrangements for MBBS and BDS. Applicants will be required to provide their personal and identification details, academic qualifications, MDCAT information and supporting documentation. These documents may include Matriculation and HSSC certificates, identity records, domicile certificates and equivalence documents, where applicable. Candidates applying against reserved categories must also submit the supporting evidence required for their respective admission category. Once the required details have been entered, applicants must select their preferred colleges, generate the admission processing fee challan and complete the prescribed payment and final submission procedures. UHS has warned that incomplete applications or failure to meet the notified requirements may result in rejection. Successful candidates must subsequently fulfil the joining and payment requirements applicable to their allotted institution. What the new policy means for future dentists For students aiming to enter the dental profession, the 2026–27 policy establishes a clear framework for admissions while underlining the competitive and administrative challenges involved in securing a place. The 50 per cent MDCAT qualifying threshold provides a defined minimum for BDS eligibility, but academic performance, college preferences and seat availability will ultimately determine where successful candidates are offered admission. The December application window also gives prospective public-sector BDS candidates a distinct admission timeline, separate from the earlier MBBS process. For private dental college applicants, early financial planning will be essential, particularly because the initial Rs600,000 deposit must be paid within a short period following selection. Candidates are strongly advised to consult the official notification, monitor UHS announcements and review institutional preferences carefully before submitting their applications. The complete admission policy, relevant prospectus and official notices can be accessed through the University of Health Sciences Lahore website at https://www.uhs.edu.pk/. headline: Dubai Chambers signs four MoUs with Chinese chambers
snippet: DUBAI: Dubai Chambers has signed Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with four chambers of commerce in China to strengthen cooperation, support the business community, and deepen ties between companies in Dubai and their counterparts in Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and Chongqing. Dubai Chambers signed the agreements with the Beijing Chamber of International Commerce (BCIC), the China Chamber of International Commerce Shenzhen Branch (CCOIC Shenzhen), the China Chamber of International Commerce Guangzhou Chamber of Commerce (CCOIC Guangzhou), and the China Chamber of International Commerce Chongqing Chamber of Commerce (CCOIC Chongqing). The agreements were signed during the Dubai Business Forum - China, organised recently by Dubai Chambers in Shenzhen. Mohammad Ali Rashed Lootah, President and CEO of Dubai Chambers, signed the MoUs with Zhang Jianwei, Chairperson of the Beijing Chamber of International Commerce; Huang Xiaofeng, Vice President of CCOIC Guangzhou; and Deng Lin, Vice Chairwoman of CCOIC Chongqing. The MoU with CCOIC Shenzhen was signed by Salem AlShamsi, Executive Vice President of International Relations at Dubai Chambers, and He Shanshan, Secretary-General of CCOIC Shenzhen. Lootah said Dubai Chambers was committed to strengthening ties with priority markets by building partnerships that facilitate direct engagement between businesses and create new trade and investment opportunities. "At the same time, we are developing a supportive ecosystem that enables the local private sector to expand its international presence and benefit from the exchange of expertise and knowledge. This enhances the ability of companies to connect with new partners, build sustainable business relationships, and achieve strong performance that contributes to the growth of trade and investment between Dubai and global markets," he added. The MoUs aim to strengthen relations, support the development of broader trade and economic ties, and enhance cooperation between companies. The agreement with CCOIC Chongqing also focuses on promoting trade and investment, facilitating the exchange of information on international exhibitions, economic and trade meetings, and other commercial activities, and providing mutual support for participation in these events. The agreements reinforce Dubai Chambers’ role in building effective channels of cooperation with trade and investment institutions across international markets. They provide a framework for stronger engagement between companies and support the development of mutually beneficial trade and investment relationships. The MoUs also create practical channels for exchanging information and expertise, exploring opportunities of mutual interest, and enabling Dubai’s business community to expand its international networks and establish high-value partnerships that support growth and expansion. These efforts form part of Dubai Chambers’ strategy to enhance the competitiveness of the private sector, broaden its access to international markets, and support its contribution to sustainable economic growth in Dubai.

headline: Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal
snippet: As one walks along the beachfront of Barcelona, the shoreline feels like it has always been there: sand, palm trees, a long promenade, restaurants, shops and modern hotels, when the reality is that it has not always been this way. Until the 1980s, Barcelona's seafront was a working barrier of railway lines, factories and informal housing, and wastewater ran straight into the Mediterranean. Starting in 1987, Barcelona has continuously created large promenades and passages between the city and the sea, creating an environment that today many might read as previously empty space, but is actually the result of decades of infrastructure and social complexity, along with a municipal effort to transform the city's territory and its relationship to the water. Following that transformation raises three questions that frame this article: who was displaced to open the waterfront, who governs it today, and who keeps it standing?
